cases.name: implementation-model-cli-taxonomy
cases.trap: Designer produces an IA that mirrors the system's internal service or module structure rather than user mental models — CLI commands are named after internal services, organizational units, or database entities instead of the tasks users are trying to accomplish.
cases.prompt: We're building a CLI tool for a SaaS platform. The backend has three internal services: AuthService, DataPipelineOrchestrator, and NotificationDispatcher. The engineering team has proposed this command structure: `saas-cli authservice login`, `saas-cli authservice create-token`, `saas-cli datapipelineorchestrator run`, `saas-cli datapipelineorchestrator list-runs`, `saas-cli notificationdispatcher send`, `saas-cli notificationdispatcher list-channels`. Design the IA for this CLI.
expectations: Designer must identify that the proposed structure mirrors internal service names (AuthService, DataPipelineOrchestrator, NotificationDispatcher) rather than user task vocabulary
Designer must produce an alternative namespace that uses the user's mental model — what the user is working with (auth, pipeline, notifications) in language users would use
Designer must explain why mirroring internal service names fails: users approaching the CLI to 'run my pipeline' will not know to look under 'datapipelineorchestrator'
The proposed IA must use the noun-verb or verb-noun pattern consistently — not mixed between services
Designer must apply the information-scent test to the top-level namespace: would a user who has never read the documentation know which top-level command to start with for each common task?
Designer must produce a controlled vocabulary for the command namespace — resolving any synonyms (e.g., is 'run' or 'execute' the canonical verb for running a pipeline?)
negative_expectations: Designer must not accept 'authservice', 'datapipelineorchestrator', or 'notificationdispatcher' as user-facing command names without questioning whether these match user vocabulary
Designer must not produce an IA that requires users to know internal service names to find commands — this is implementation-model IA
Designer must not omit the information-scent evaluation — the test 'would a user know what is inside this namespace?' must be applied to the proposed top-level commands

cases.name: mystery-meat-navigation-labels
cases.trap: Designer accepts or produces navigation labels that are marketing vocabulary — 'Solutions', 'Resources', 'Insights', 'Engage' — or similarly vague labels that create no information scent, and treats them as acceptable navigation because they sound professional or match the brand voice.
cases.prompt: We're designing the top-level navigation for a B2B SaaS product that helps engineering teams manage their cloud infrastructure. The product manager has proposed this navigation: 'Home | Solutions | Resources | Insights | Settings'. The PM says the words test well with marketing and 'feel premium'. Design the IA for this navigation.
expectations: Designer must identify each of the proposed labels as mystery meat navigation and name why each fails the information-scent test
Designer must apply the information-scent test explicitly: 'Would a user who has never visited this product know what they will find under Solutions? Under Resources? Under Insights?'
Designer must produce alternative labels that use the actual content vocabulary — what the user will find, in the user's task language
Designer must distinguish between what labels 'feel like' (brand voice, premium tone) and what labels accomplish (creating accurate expectations before the click)
Designer must produce at least one scenario showing how a user would fail to find something they need because the navigation labels do not predict the content
The proposed navigation labels must be specific enough that a user could predict which label to click for at least 3 different user tasks
negative_expectations: Designer must not accept 'Solutions', 'Resources', or 'Insights' as navigation labels without applying the information-scent test
Designer must not treat 'feels premium' or 'tests well with marketing' as a valid argument for navigation labels — marketing testing and navigation findability testing are different
Designer must not produce replacement labels that are still ambiguous — replacing 'Solutions' with 'Products' when the content is actually 'Infrastructure monitoring tools' is not an improvement

cases.name: web-ia-applied-to-tui-without-surface-translation
cases.trap: Designer applies web navigation IA patterns (breadcrumbs, global nav bars, horizontal tabs) to a TUI design problem without translating them to terminal-appropriate navigation mechanisms — treating TUI as a text-rendered GUI rather than a distinct surface with distinct navigation constraints.
cases.prompt: We're designing a TUI application for managing Kubernetes clusters. The application needs to let users navigate between: cluster overview, namespace list, pod details, service list, and deployment history. The designer has proposed: a breadcrumb trail at the top showing 'Clusters > Namespaces > Pods', a horizontal tab bar for switching between resource types, and a sidebar with global navigation. Design the IA for this TUI.
expectations: Designer must identify that breadcrumbs, horizontal tab bars, and sidebars are web/desktop navigation patterns that require translation for TUI implementation

Designer must address the TUI-specific navigation model: key bindings are navigation, the status bar shows current position, the view hierarchy is expressed through pane structure rather than visual navigation bars

Designer must produce a view hierarchy showing what views exist and what the navigation relationships between them are — which views are sibling levels, which are parent-child, which are modal overlays
Designer must distinguish view state (which namespace is selected in the list) from navigation (moving from the namespace list view to a pod detail view)
Designer must specify what wayfinding mechanisms replace breadcrumbs in the TUI context — the status bar content, the current view title, the navigation indicators visible at all times
The IA must address the 'orphaned view' risk: every view must have a discoverable path in (how to reach it) and a way out (how to navigate back)
negative_expectations: Designer must not propose a breadcrumb trail without addressing how breadcrumbs work in a terminal grid — they cannot be clicked, and the visual representation is different from web
Designer must not treat a horizontal tab bar as a navigation solution without addressing terminal rendering constraints (fixed-cell grid, no CSS, limited color depth)

Designer must not produce an IA that applies web navigation vocabulary ('links', 'pages', 'clicking navigation items') without translating to TUI equivalents ('key bindings', 'views', 'focus movement')

cases.name: over-categorization-future-proofing
cases.trap: Designer creates a deeply nested category structure with thin categories (1-3 items each) justified by anticipated future content growth — producing an IA where users must navigate through empty-feeling levels to reach content, because the structure was designed for content that does not yet exist.
cases.prompt: We're designing the settings structure for a developer tool. Currently the tool has 8 settings: editor font size, editor color theme, editor line numbers toggle, git commit auto-sign, git default branch name, notifications for deploys, notifications for failures, and API key. The product manager wants the settings organized into: 'Editor > Appearance > Typography' (font size), 'Editor > Appearance > Themes' (color theme), 'Editor > Appearance > Display' (line numbers), 'Editor > Version Control > Git > Commits' (auto-sign), 'Editor > Version Control > Git > Branches' (default branch), 'Integrations > Notifications > Deploys' (deploy notifications), 'Integrations > Notifications > Failures' (failure notifications), 'Security > Authentication > API Access' (API key). The PM says this structure is 'future-proof'. Design the IA for these settings.
expectations: Designer must identify that the proposed structure has over-categorization: most leaf nodes contain exactly 1 item, and the hierarchy is 3-4 levels deep for 8 settings
Designer must apply the over-categorization test: how many items does each category currently contain? Would flattening the structure harm findability?
Designer must propose an alternative structure calibrated to the existing content — not the anticipated future content
Designer must explain the cognitive cost of over-categorization: users must navigate through 3-4 hierarchy levels to reach a single setting, which is more effort than scanning a flat list of 8 items
Designer must distinguish between depth that serves findability (when there are genuinely too many items at one level) and depth that serves anticipated future organization
The proposed IA must explain the principle: design for what exists, with the simplest structure that doesn't actively prevent future growth
negative_expectations: Designer must not accept 'future-proof' as sufficient justification for deep nesting of thin categories
Designer must not produce an IA with 3+ hierarchy levels for content that could be organized in 1-2 levels without harming findability
Designer must not recommend the proposed structure without applying the user-effort test: is the navigation cost of 3-4 clicks to reach a single setting justified by the organizational benefit?
